narrative:
The model predicts you have a 42% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The prediction is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed two classes in the past. Among students who passed, the average number of previous failures is zero, so this history strongly pushes the model toward expecting you will fail again. The second most important factor is that your guardian is someone other than your mother or father. This is quite unusual—only 1.7% of students who passed have a guardian listed as “other”—and it pulls the prediction slightly toward passing, perhaps because the model sees it as a sign of extra external support. Finally, your very low weekend alcohol consumption also nudges the outcome a little toward passing, since most students who succeed also report low or very low weekend drinking.

Even though two of these factors work in your favor, your past failures outweigh them and drive the overall prediction that you are at serious risk. To improve, you should focus first on breaking the pattern of failing classes. Speak with your teachers about targeted help in the subjects that have been hardest for you, create a realistic weekly study schedule (most successful students study at least two hours per week), and make full use of the remedial courses now available to you. Small, consistent changes in study habits can still change the outcome before final exams.
